The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials.

They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster. The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA.

It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.

The Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute.

"The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," SETI wrote of the broadcast in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's."

The message was designed by astronomy professor Frank Drake of Cornell University (who also developed the famed Drake Equation for alien life), as well as Cornnell graduate students Richard Isaacman and Linda May, and Arecibo staff member James Walker, with input from astronomer Carl Sagan and others, according to Cornell University.

The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers, with the broadcast lasting less than 3 minutes, according to SETI.

As of 2026, the message should have traveled about 52 light-years (1 light-year is the distance light travels in a year), with 24,948 light-years to go before reaching star cluster M13.

The Arecibo message may have been the first message of its kind, but it wasn't the last. We have also included messages on several spacecraft, such as Pioneer and Voyager. NASA and Paul McCartney also beamed a performance of "Across the Universe" in 2008.

#771. Shevchenko accuses Mudryk camp of 'baseless slander'

Mykhailo Mudryk has won 28 caps for Ukraine

Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for an employee of the country's football federation to "falsely" take the blame for the winger's positive drugs test.

Tottenham winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.

The 25-year-old said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.

In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk firmly placed the blame for his 20-month absence from the sport on his national association, which has led to Shevchenko's response.

In a statement, former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko, who is now president of the UAF, said Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally" and called on the player to retract his words.

He added: "His representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to find an employee who would falsely take responsibility for the meldonium found in his doping sample.

"The UAF refused, as such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work."

He added that "numerous investigations and audits" undertaken as part of the case were unable to shed light on when or where the substance entered Mudryk's system.

In his interview Mudryk also claimed Shevchenko had offered him little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and said its handling of the matter delayed his return to football.

However, Shevchenko went on to say that national team staff had complied with a request from Chelsea not to provide Mudryk with any medication while on international duty.

And he also challenged the former Shakhtar Donetsk forward to provide evidence "to back up his words".

"Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also approved for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him at the training camps," Shevchenko added.

"These were the exact people who monitored his regimen and recovery, and helped him with his daily routine.

"The UAF completed all necessary checks in this case. We provided Mudryk's representatives with the information they requested and remained in contact with those working on the case.

"I know the people who have worked with the national team for many years. I trust them, because throughout all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make anyone doubt their professionalism.

"If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it. If no such evidence exists, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he has called into question."

BBC Sport has contacted Mudryk's representatives for comment.

#770. Frank happy to be 'back in the circus' at Palace

Thomas Frank replaces Frenchman Pierre Sage at Crystal Palace

Thomas Frank is happy to be "back in the circus" after speaking at his first news conference as Crystal Palace manager.

The 53-year-old, who was appointed on a two-and-a-half-year deal on Monday, has been out of worked since he was sacked by Tottenham in February, less than eight months after taking the job.

But, rather than dwell on that disappointment, Frank hopes to use it as a learning exeprience as he attempts to improve Palace's fortunes and lift them off the bottom of the Premier League table.

"If you don't learn from any of your jobs, I don't think you reflect, I don't think you improve, and I don't think you get better," said Frank.

"Of course there's a lot of things I have been reflecting over. The details, that will be for another time, but I can say I've learned, definitely."

The Dane said he could easily have extended his break from football, which he used to travel to Japan and Australia, as well as "visiting friends and family, eating too well [and] drinking too much wine" back in his homeland.

"I was very aware I didn't want to do anything in the summer. I put a statement out there, I needed more time," he added.

"I can actually, honestly say I would have been fine if it was three, four, five, six, seven months more, because it's good to be back in the circus, but it's also unbelievably good not to be in, especially if you enjoy life, which I do.

"I was spending time with family and friends and doing all that, but I think the club, the way Palace is, how well Steve Parish especially spoke about the club and ideas, Matt Hobbs and Iain Moody and these guys, too, helped convince me it was a good idea.

"I'm a little bit surprised by this feeling I have in the body, how good it feels."

How Frank can restore reputation and save Crystal Palace

Frank's Palace reign begins with a trip to Coventry City on Saturday (15:00 GMT) and he says he returns to the dugout unbruised despite the way his stint at Spurs ended.

"I think we all have an ego," the former Brentford boss said. "Some are better at controlling it than others. For me, it's not the critics, it's more what I can learn, what I can prove, how I can get better.

"There's a lot of clever people out there, but the interesting thing is they only know 10 per cent of the truth. That's a tenth of the truth at Brentford, there's a tenth of the truth at Tottenham, and that's just the way it is.

"If you can't handle that as a coach or a player, then you shouldn't be in this business, and I'm very happy to be back in the game."

#769. DWTS’ Val Chmerkovskiy Makes Spicy Comment About Jenna Johnson's Exit

Dancing With the Stars pro Val Chmerkovskiy expressed his support for wife Jenna Johnson following their back-to-back eliminations by giving an NSFW shoutout to his “baddie” wife.

Val Chmerkovskiy and Jenna Johnson may not be adding another Mirrorball to their household, but they're still having a ball at home.

A day after Johnson and her partner Harry Shum Jr. were voted off Dancing With the Stars following his and his partner Jenna Dewan’s elimination the week prior, Chmerkovskiy showed his support for his wife with a steamy comment.

“Keep the trophy’s [sic],” the 40-year-old shared on his Instagram Stories Nov. 18 alongside a photo of Johnson from a red carpet event. “I get to watch this baddie brush her teeth naked every morning.” Chmerkovskiy—who shares son Rome, 3, with his wife of seven years—also thirsted after her by adding a drool emoji.

Johnson and Shum were shockingly sent home on the Nov. 17 semifinals after receiving perfect scores 30 out of 30 for both of their dances: a paso doble to Rihanna's "We Found Love” and a quickstep to Amy Winehouse's “Valerie,” in which Shum paid tribute to late Glee costar Naya Rivera.

While some believe viewers made a major misstep by sending the pair home, the duo slammed the negativity they said they received online, sharing they think it impacted their relationship with the rest of the season 35 cast.

“I hope to get to know them more,” Shum told E! News in an interview following their elimination Nov. 17, “because it's just been so chaotic.”

“We're a bit all trauma bonded,” Johnson chimed in, to which Shum added, “There's a lot of trauma bond just because this year has been a little crazy.”

“Social media is a little nuts,” he continued. “I hope they address that at a certain point, because I think there's a good amount of bullying that doesn't feel really good, and I think the rest of the cast feels it.”

Though Shum didn’t go into specifics, he and Johnson were spun into drama after Chmerkovskiy received a one-week suspension from the show following his now-infamous reaction to a critique judge Carrie Ann Inaba made after one of Johnson and Shum’s performances, in which he referenced Will Smith’s 2022 Oscar slap.

Shum seemingly referred to the fallout as he praised Johnson after they were voted off.

“I want to say you have been dealing with everything with grace, with the noise outside,” the Grey’s Anatomy star told his partner on air, “and teaching me the things that I have only dreamed of to learn, and this has been one of the most beautiful experiences. So, thank you so much.”

As DWTS prepares to tango into its season 35 finale, read on for a deep dive into the secrets of the ballroom…

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones said he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality said on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last."

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show."

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

"You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody."

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together."

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay said on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'"

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna said on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner."

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

"It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well."

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again."

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers."

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee said pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and new in something different every week, so it stays interesting."

More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.

That's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that currently circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). Analyzing data from Oct. 12 and 18 this year, researchers found that with a completely unobstructed horizon, 710 satellites were crossing the sky in every single moment of the night above an average U.K. town.

The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S. Space Force available through the public website CelesTrak. Although the researchers specifically focused on the U.K., they say that such heavy satellite traffic flows above most of Europe, the U.S. and other mid-latitude regions, especially between 40 and 50 degrees north or south.

"Most Starlink satellites orbit at around 53 degrees to the equator, so the satellites bunch up over the mid-latitudes. These worldwide figures are approximate, based on a global grid over a single day," Accu Components spokesperson told Space.com in an email. "Skies near the equator are the quietest, with around 490 satellites."

Not all of those satellites are visible to the naked eye, the researchers said in a statement. Because satellites unlike stars don't produce their own light, they must be illuminated by the sun, while the ground below has already sunk into darkness, to be visible. According to the study, an average of 105 satellites out of those 710 were catching light as they zoomed overhead, shining as bright as stars.

The spokesperson said that the actual number of visible satellites varies drastically throughout the night. During the hours after dusk and before dawn, a much greater number of satellites can be seen, while in the middle of the night most no longer catch any light.

"For a typical U.K. town, around 300 satellites are catching the sunlight in the first hour or so after dark," the spokesperson said. "That falls to fewer than 20 around midnight, then climbs back to around 300 before dawn."

For comparison, as little as a few dozen stars are visible to the naked eye in the dead of the night above large, light-polluted megalopolis such as London or New York, according to OwnStarMap. In suburban areas and smaller towns, that number grows to a few hundred. To get to a few thousand visible stars, one must retreat into remote countryside or isolated mountain ranges.

The number of satellites orbiting Earth has grown steeply in the past decade, especially since Elon Musk’s SpaceX began launching its internet-beaming Starlink constellation. Satellite companies plan to launch hundreds of thousands, possibly millions of satellites in the coming decades. If those visions come to pass, the number of passing satellites will vastly outgrow that of stars almost anywhere in the world. The trend especially concerns astronomers who fear the impacts on humankind’s ability to study the Universe.

Satellites crossing the view of ground-based telescopes leave streaks in astronomical images and increase the overall brightness of the sky through the light they reflect down towards Earth. Gradually, even the most powerful telescopes could lose their ability to see the distant stars and galaxies that hold the answers to key questions about the history of the universe.

The study found that throughout the night, an average U.K. town sees 12,891 different satellites passing overhead.

Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

#767. VPR's Jax Taylor Experiencing Complications After Cancer Surgery

Jax Taylor experienced "complications” that have delayed his release from the hospital following kidney cancer surgery, a source close to Vanderpump Rules alum exclusively told E! News.

Jax Taylor has hit a small roadblock in his recovery from kidney cancer surgery.

The Vanderpump Rules alum's release from the hospital has been delayed due to after experiencing "some complications," a source close to Taylor exclusively told E! News Nov. 19.

"Physically, he’s very sore from the incisions," the source said, "but mentally, he’s feeling relieved to have the surgery behind him, as it’s something that’s been weighing heavily on him for months."

Fortunately, Taylor is surrounded by a strong support system, including his girlfriend Lori Krebs.

"Lori has been by his side," the source shared. "The last few months have really taken a toll on him and she’s always been someone who brings him a sense of peace. They’ve been through a lot together and there’s a very deep love and connection between them."

The insider added, "They’re truly there for one another, and I think going through something like this has only made them realize just how much they mean to each other."

Taylor, who confirmed his relationship with Krebs earlier this year, had been privately navigating his cancer diagnosis for a while before going public with his health journey. As he shared in a Nov. 19 Instagram post, “This is something I’ve kept private for the past few months because it’s been one of the scariest times of my life."

“What I thought was just a kidney stone turned into something I never imagined," the 47-year-old wrote. "My CT scan also showed a tumor on my left kidney. After many tests and appointments I found out it was cancer.”

Ultimately, Taylor underwent a five-hour surgery to have the tumor removed. While the medical crisis put the Valley star in "a really dark place," he credited Krebs for being his guiding light.

“I honestly don’t know how I would have gotten through everything without my amazing girlfriend by my side,” shared Taylor, who's dad to 5-year-old son Cruz with ex Brittany Cartwright. “She’s been my rock through all of this."

He added, "She’s not just my partner, she’s my best friend and I feel so insanely lucky to have her in my life."

#766. Arsenal 'have ingredients' but Europe's elite on another level

Arsenal goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez made six saves but was beaten twice in defeat by Lyon

It is only 18 months since Arsenal tasted European glory, but they are not a team on many people's list of favourites for this season's Women's Champions League.

That is because not only have the Gunners disappointed across their opening 15 matches of the season, but also the elite teams in Europe seem to have gone up another level.

In the space of seven days, Arsenal have witnessed first hand what it takes to reach those heights - and the gap they must bridge.

Last week, they were resilient at Barcelona to earn a very respectable 1-1 draw, but were fortunate the Spanish side were not clinical with their chances at Camp Nou.

On Thursday night, they were outplayed at home in losing 2-0 to an excellent Lyon side, who look on course to match or better their runner-up finish from last season.

One point from such games could be pleasing - but that only shows the work Arsenal need to do to be considered one of the top teams in Europe.

French giants Lyon outclass Arsenal in Women's Champions League

Arsenal came into Thursday's defeat by Lyon off the back of a fifth successive Women's Super League draw at Emirates Stadium against London City Lionesses.

In contrast, Lyon have been flying domestically, winning all nine of their matches, scoring 49 goals, and then not conceding any in their unbeaten Champions League run.

Such form sets the pace and it was clear at Meadow Park that they were superior to Arsenal in every department.

Vibrant Germany international Jule Brand gave them the lead midway through the first half and Melchie Dumornay sealed the win with a powerful strike in the 57th minute.

Arsenal defender Leah Williamson said the "better team won the game" and manager Renee Slegers highlighted the difference in physicality between the teams.

"Compared to last year when we played Lyon [in the semi-finals], they are even better now. They have standout individual quality," Slegers said.

"They dominated in the first half. We had solutions for the second half and had more presence. We wore them down better but it still didn't lead to open chances."

Despite playing at right-back, Jule Brand had the third most touches in the Arsenal penalty area for Lyon (five) after striker Marie-Antoinette Katoto and fellow goalscorer Melchie Dumornay

Lyon had a 3.33 expected goals ratio on Thursday, serving up 23 shots to Arsenal's seven. They created six big chances and 14 of their shots were inside the box.

Dumornay oozed quality, midfielder Lily Yohannes showed composure and Brand was very impressive both defensively and going forward for Lyon, deployed in a new position.

Those individuals have benefitted from the expertise of former Barcelona manager Jonatan Giraldez, who joined in June 2025 - the month after Arsenal won the Champions League - and has now had the time he needed to impose his style.

As a result, Lyon have gone up another level and the gap between these two teams has widened by Arsenal's drop-off this season.

Slegers also said Arsenal had "prepared all we could" for the intensity that Lyon brought in London - but it still did not have an impact.

Asked how far off Lyon they currently are, Slegers said: "It's 2-0 today and they are better than us but it doesn't mean if we were to play them again soon, this season, that it would be the same game again.

"We saw moments where we did well and we know from the last couple of years we can hurt Lyon.

"But for today, their pace and physicality helped them get too much dominance in the game and that is one of their strengths. Then it became hard for us."

Arsenal have not yet qualified for the knockout stages of the Champions League

Williamson said Arsenal "know what they need to do to be better" and that they are aware of "where the gaps are" to Europe's elite.

They are already 12 points off the pace in the Women's Super League title race and are unlikely to qualify automatically for the Champions League quarter-finals.

"The level rises year on year. Everybody cops goals - we have to try not to and we have to create," said Williamson following the defeat by Lyon.

"We're all focused and we're all together. That's the most comforting thing for me - but this has been a tough period."

It has not all been bad despite disappointing results - and context is important.

Over a gruelling seven days, they have faced European holders Barcelona, WSL high-flyers London City Lionesses and record Champions League winners Lyon.

They showed grit and resilience out in Barcelona last week - traits that have not been on show enough for Arsenal this season, but are clearly there.

Players like Williamson, striker Alessia Russo and summer signings Georgia Stanway and Ona Batlle know what it takes to compete at the highest level.

Arsenal invested in the summer transfer window and brought in proven, experienced players, but that has not translated into results - yet.

Giraldez said time with his players has helped improve Lyon and perhaps that is what Arsenal need - patience.

"I think they are changing now. They made a good game against Barcelona and it's very difficult to go there and get a point," said Giraldez.

"The game against London City was much better. It's not just about them, but also about us. Now we have improved and play better football than last year.

"I think it is a matter of time [for Arsenal]. They have a good coach and good players. In general, they have all the ingredients to have a good season."

#765. Culture, defence, Fernandes - Pochettino's priorities at Man Utd

Mauricio Pochettino's first game as Manchester United head coach will be at Liverpool on 22 November

"We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."

Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the club.

The former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea boss wasted no time getting across the Atlantic Ocean after completing his stint in charge of the United States on Tuesday.

He met key staff on Wednesday, took training for the first time on Thursday and conducts his first wider media conference at United's Carrington training ground on Friday.

The 54-year-old is facing a packed schedule, starting with a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.

Pochettino accepted a big challenge. United are 18th in the table. By 17:00 GMT on Saturday, they could be bottom.

So, what are the Argentine's priorities as he begins the task of trying to transform United's season?

"To create the culture is the most important [thing]," he told United's in-house media in a 15-minute introductory chat.

Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator

Manchester won't always be blue - Pochettino

Fitness obsessed & 'control freak' - what can Man Utd expect from Pochettino?

Matheus Cunha's injury-time goal against Roma on 3 November sealed one of only three Manchester United victories in 15 games this season

It would be easy to point to areas of the pitch where United have been deficient this season. However, it cannot be totally dismissed that virtually the same group of players were transformed over the second half of last season by the recently sacked Michael Carrick, who guided them to third in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.

Remarkably, Pochettino has won twice as many matches in charge of the USA this season than the three victories United have managed, with a 100% record from six games.

United, by contrast, have not won in the Premier League since August, while two of their three victories have required the Red Devils to come from behind. Their single clean sheet came against Azerbaijan outfit Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.

One of the most immediate tasks for Pochettino will be to alter the mindset of players who seem to have become restricted by the pressure they have found themselves subjected to.

"It is a mistake to see the situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club.

"We need to understand it is a game, and to connect with the game we need to feel free. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is our priority now; to work with them and take the pressure.

"Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."

Diogo Dalot is consoled by Manchester United team-mate Joshua Zirkzee after being substituted during the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa

That said, there are some glaring issues that Carrick was unable to fix and Pochettino must find an answer to. The most obvious is defence.

Who should the cornerstones of United's defence be?

The Carrick regime felt Leny Yoro was the player with the attributes - pace, strength and control - most suited to their needs. Yet, at 21, Yoro is prone to mistakes and he has also been needed at right-back because regular right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have, at times, been required on the left.

Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt have not been reliable fitness wise. Pochettino knows the baggage attached to Martinez, given his post-match criticisms of the club hierarchy after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid, and the knowledge his fellow countryman's contract expires in the summer.

Harry Maguire has started all 10 league games this season but suffered a back spasm in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, immediately before the international break, and had to be replaced at half-time. Maguire has many attributes, but his presence does restrict the ability to press high up the field.

Ayden Heaven has made eight appearances in all competitions but has previously been regarded as being behind Yoro in terms of his overall development.

The 27-year-old was consoled by Joshua Zirkzee when he was replaced against Villa, such was the negative fan reaction to his performance, which included conceding a penalty at the start of the second-half.

It can justifiably be argued if Dalot has the talent to match the 260 club appearances he has now made.

However, for his faults, coaches love his attitude.

Dalot has been described to BBC Sport as having one of the most committed and professional approaches to the game, that he is someone willing to take responsibility, happy to play in unfamiliar positions if it benefits the team, the first to offer support to team-mates, and a positive influence in the dressing room.

Liverpool and Man Utd fans give predictions ahead of Premier League match

Bruno Fernandes' alarming drop off in form has been one of the most noticeable features of the current campaign.

The Portugal playmaker has been a shadow of the star who scooped all the player of the year awards last season and broke the Premier League assist record.

He was axed for the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth after criticising Carrick's tactics in the 4-1 Champions League humiliation by Como and seems to be affected by concerns around his future - his contract also expires in the summer, although United are almost certain to trigger their one-year option on the 32-year-old - and the summer arrival of Youri Tielemans.

For the short term at least, Pochettino must decide whether to pick Fernandes in his favoured number 10 role and work around that, or drop him deeper, as Ruben Amorim did, or play him wide, which has not brought the best out of him.

Why does Pochettino keep lemons in his office?

Fernandes' status affects other areas. Carrick never seemed convinced by Andrey Santos, a Â£50m summer arrival from Chelsea. But with Â£70m Carlos Baleba out for an extended period, a partner needs to be found in midfield for Kobbie Mainoo.

Tielemans did not seem to have the running ability for the role, and Amorim wouldn't pick Mainoo with Fernandes.

Further forward, with Benjamin Sesko out, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo have tended to be used in the number nine role. But Cunha likes to drop deep, while, after a bright start to the season, Mbeumo has scored twice in his past 12 appearances.

Neither Shea Lacey nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season. Both caught the eye on England Under-20 duty during the international break. Pochettino has history for giving young players a chance and the pair could benefit from that.

Manchester United co-chair Avram Glazer and minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe have been the subject of numerous supporter protests and chants

There is one issue Pochettino mentioned in his interview he will soon discover requires delicate handling.

United's match-going fans have stood by every manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired. There is no reason to think that will change now.

However, their relationship with the club's ownership is fractured, possibly beyond repair. Fresh accounts to 30 September show the club's overall debt remains more than Â£1.1bn and a further Â£14.5m was spent on finance costs in the previous quarter.

This fuels discontent in the stands, already heightened because of various ticketing measures, none of which are viewed by most supporters as being positive.

"Chemistry is really important, chemistry between us and the staff and the fans and the players, the directors, the owners and everything."

#764. Reflect Orbital wants to launch thousands of sunlight-beaming mirrors to space — and the 1st will go up next year

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

"This lighting will support a variety of customers, from remote search-and-rescue operations to solar farms generating clean power."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Reflect Orbital is moving forward with its plan to place mirrors in Earth orbit to produce and sell sunlight after dark.

The goal is to extend the hours and output of solar farms globally, "making clean power dispatchable and available when you need it," the California-based startup explains on its website.

Reflect Orbital has made significant progress to date. On Tuesday (Nov. 10), for example, the company announced it had secured $73.5 million in new funding, boosting its total raise to more than $100 million. It has also gotten a formal go-ahead from the U.S. government to try out the concept in space and is currently readying its first test satellite, which is expected to launch in the second quarter of 2027. The identity of the launch provider is being kept under wraps at this time, the firm told Space.com.

Reflect Orbital recently conducted a ground-based test in California, lighting up a mountainous area to practice search and rescue (SAR) techniques.

On Oct. 10, the space startup set up spotlights near Lone Pine, California to simulate the illumination its proposed satellites could provide — controlled lighting without the need for any ground infrastructure. "This lighting will support a variety of customers, from remote search-and-rescue operations to solar farms generating clean power," the company explained in an Oct. 14 statement.

The October illumination test ran from 7 p.m. to midnight and involved members of the China Lake Mountain Rescue Group (CLMRG), who practiced with night-time equipment.

CLMRG is an all-volunteer activity, operating under the auspices of the Kern County Sheriff's Office providing SAR services on an on-call basis at no cost.

"Together with local search-and-rescue and disaster response groups, we carried out a fully permitted nighttime demonstration of our responsive lighting service," a Reflect Orbital spokesperson told Space.com in response to an inquiry about the exercise. "Search-and-rescue and disaster response teams are expected to be our first customers, so this was a real-world test conducted alongside teams who will use our technology."

Mobile lighting gear was mounted on Horseshoe Meadows Road to provide a spot of light similar to the ones that Reflect Orbital satellites are expected to deliver. "The aim was to create a precise, realistic simulation of our service, so emergency responders could see how it will perform in real scenarios," Reflect Orbital said.

The brightness of the spot was roughly 0.7 lumens.

Reflect Orbital added that it will keep working closely with local communities and authorities wherever the company operates, to show how its technology can help save lives.

"We're committed to learning incrementally about our technology and its impacts, and from potential customers and stakeholders, ahead of our planned satellite operations," the company stated.

In last month's illumination experiment, Reflect Orbital secured permits in advance, filed a NOTAM (a notice to pilots), notified Edwards Air Force Base and coordinated with the local sheriff's department. Area residents were also notified about the test ahead of time.

In a related development, Reflect Orbital has announced the purchase of two Skyroot Aerospace launches to deploy some of its spacecraft. Skyroot's Vikram-1 launcher is a product of India's private space sector, first flying from the nation's Sriharikota launch site last July. That flight was a landmark success, as Vikram-1 became the first private Indian rocket ever to reach orbit.

"These dedicated launches provide assured schedule and capacity, and complement Reflect Orbital's other planned launches from sites in the United States," Reflect Orbital explained in a different Oct. 14 statement.

Reflect Orbital says its approach is "incremental and test-and-learn." The company has been granted a license from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for one satellite. That mission will test the technology, including built-in safeguards governing precisely how, where and when the sunlight service is delivered.

"It will provide real-world data that shapes the design of future satellites," Reflect Orbital said, "the markets we serve, how we engage communities and the operational practices we put in place. We expect this to be the first of several test missions."

Reflect Orbital wants to be operating at least 50,000 of its mirror satellites in orbit by 2035. Not surprisingly, many people in the astronomy and stargazer communities have a dim view of this plan, saying it will generate light pollution that significantly degrades the night sky.

Reflect Orbital counters that most people and most places will never see this light. Customers will require permits, signoff from local authorities and "Know Your Customer compliance" to receive the service. Every service will require multi-layer approval, the company says, and if people do not want the light, they will not receive it.

Reflect Orbital also claims that it can maintain exclusion zones covering astronomical observation sites.

"Our satellites will be default-off when idle and constellation vehicles are designed to stay under +7 stellar magnitude for all non-serving attitudes. We're able to dim the brightness of the service and turn it off at any stage," the company's website states.

Reflect Orbital also notes that it's an industry member of the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Center for the Protection of the Dark and Quiet Sky.

The company says that it's collaborating with the IAU on an observing campaign for when the service is operational and is also working on a coordination agreement with the U.S. National Science Foundation.

"We've engaged extensively with scientists, astronomers, environmental researchers and other stakeholders," Reflect Orbital stated. "Their feedback has meaningfully informed the design of our spacecraft and operational plans. We continue to welcome scientific exploration of how novel technology could deliver a lot of benefits to the world."

Leonard David is an award-winning space journalist who has been reporting on space activities for more than 50 years. Currently writing as Space.com's Space Insider Columnist among his other projects, Leonard has authored numerous books on space exploration, Mars missions and more, with his latest being "Moon Rush: The New Space Race" published in 2019 by National Geographic. He also wrote "Mars: Our Future on the Red Planet" released in 2016 by National Geographic. Leonard  has served as a correspondent for SpaceNews, Scientific American and Aerospace America for the AIAA. He has received many awards, including the first Ordway Award for Sustained Excellence in Spaceflight History in 2015 at the AAS Wernher von Braun Memorial Symposium. You can find out Leonard's latest project at his website and on Twitter.

#763. Why Dolly Parton’s Niece Danielle Wore Singer’s Dress to CMA Awards

Dolly Parton’s niece Danielle Parton—who is brand ambassador to her estate—attended the 2026 CMA Awards wearing a dress the county legend was meant to wear in the “Light of Clear Blue Morning” video.

A little piece of Dolly Parton was at the 2026 CMA Awards.

Nearly two months after the country music legend died, her niece Danielle Parton—who was named the brand ambassador of Dolly’s estate last month—wore a dress custom-made for the “Jolene” singer.

The all-white, fringe-forward frock was, of course, covered in rhinestones and included a trim of many colors around the low-cut neckline, bodice and skirt. Danielle, 50, paired the look with diamond jewelry and a pair of gold heeled boots at the CMA Awards Nov. 18.

“It was made for the ‘Light of Clear Blue Morning’ video that she never got to finish and get to do,” Danielle told E! News in an exclusive interview on the red carpet. “So I'm wearing it tonight in honor of her.”

And while Dolly’s niece may have been inspired by the “I Will Always Love You” singer’s wardrobe, she quickly found that her aunt Dolly’s words of wisdom have left a far greater impact.

“Almost immediately right after she passed, I gave myself one day to sit around and cry and feel pitiful about it,” Danielle continued. “Then the following day I had stuff to do, and I remember she'd always say, ‘Well, you just got to get your rear in gear and get to it.’ So that's what I did.”

But Danielle knows that Dolly’s impact goes far beyond the Parton family.

“Dolly was such an incredible human,” she said. “I'm a fan of hers as much as I am a family member, and it's always nice, especially as a family member, to see somebody in your own family have a positive impact on other people.”

As for the tribute to Dolly performed by Vince Gill and CMA host Lainey Wilson during the event, Danielle noted she was “really excited to see those that she's had such an influence on get to pay their respects in their way.”

#762. Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?

The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank has a grievance redress mechanism for people affected by projects it finances. But those seeking to file a complaint face significant hurdles. Critics say reforms are needed.

For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over.

For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods.

In late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank. It remains unclear whether this complaint will lead to an independent investigation.

The AIIB, which finances major infrastructure projects across Asia, has a mechanism in place to deal with such complaints.

Individuals who suffer adverse effects from the bank-financed projects may, under certain conditions, file a complaint with the institution.

However, access to this process — known as the Project Complaints Mechanism (PPM) — remains controversial.

According to a report by The Diplomat, a magazine that covers political and economic developments in Asia, none of the 45 complaints listed on the AIIB's website had been deemed admissible as of mid-September.

The bank acknowledged that "no cases have passed the PPM's eligibility assessment," but it stressed that this is "only part of the story."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The AIIB emphasized that not every issue needs to be resolved through this mechanism.

The PPM is "only one part of AIIB's grievance redress ecosystem," the Beijing-based bank said in response to a query from DW.

Those affected should first attempt to resolve concerns directly with the project team at the local level, it said.

According to the bank, "twelve complaints were in fact resolved at the project level — as a direct result of AIIB's follow-up and intervention — and one was resolved through domestic courts."

But critics see this as a major weakness.

"The mechanism must be easily accessible," said Arntraud Hartmann, a development economist at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS Europe) in Bologna, Italy.

She argued that people affected by the projects, for instance, are required to document potential violations of environmental and social standards from the start. "How is the affected party supposed to know which standards might have been violated?" she questioned.

The AIIB disputes this claim. "In terms of accessibility, we have made the submission form simpler and translated it into 12 languages," it said, adding that complaints can be submitted online, by phone, or by email.

Urgewald, a German environmental NGO, cites another problem with AIIB-financed projects. For many of them, information on environmental impacts and resettlements is either missing or published late, it noted.

For 2024, the NGO found that 11 of the 16 projects it examined lacked complete environmental and social impact assessments. In many cases, information on the potential number of displaced residents was also missing, it added.

"The information published on the bank's website is often insufficient and inconsistent. Particularly important documents, such as environmental impact assessments or resettlement plans, vary widely or are missing entirely," said Nora Sausmikat, a China expert at Urgewald.

The lack of information makes it difficult for those affected to respond promptly and report violations early on, she underscored, adding that the situation is particularly difficult for people without formal land titles.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Christoph Steinert, a political scientist at the University of Konstanz, said the mere existence of such grievance redressal mechanisms "is not enough."

Particularly vulnerable groups often know little about their rights, he said, adding that information should be available in local languages and targeted outreach directed at affected communities.

Criticism of the AIIB's procedures is not new. A 2023 report by international aid organizations, including Recourse, Accountability Counsel, and Inclusive Development International, revealed that the AIIB's grievance mechanism had failed to accept a single complaint since its 2019 inception.

The study highlighted that 101 of the 219 AIIB-financed projects, or 46% of the total projects at the time, were ineligible for review due to co-financing exemptions.

The AIIB typically provides funding without leading projects, a standard practice in development finance. When complaints arise, it directs complainants to the lead lender. As a result, nine of the 45 complaints fell outside its jurisdiction.

For Sausmikat, this is part of the problem. "The AIIB, however, decided against revising this requirement and established a mechanism that is very difficult to access," she said.

As of January 1, 2026, following two years of external consultations, the AIIB reformed its complaints mechanism. Under certain conditions, complaints can now be filed even while legal proceedings are ongoing.

But Sausmikat stressed that the changes are insufficient. Of the eight key recommendations made by an independent expert, only three were adopted, she underlined. "The revision did not remove the actual obstacles."

The AIIB stated that the reforms are intended to make the mechanism "more accessible and responsive."

The new rules have been in effect for only 10 months, and their implementation is being closely monitored, the bank said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Steinert said fear of reprisals poses another fundamental challenge to such procedures.

Documented cases from Latin America, for instance, show that complainants have faced administrative or legal problems, and in some cases even violence.

Such risks could deter others from filing complaints, Steinert said.  However, his research does not specifically address AIIB projects.

The bank said that it "does not tolerate retaliation against anyone who raises concerns."

"Requestors may ask for confidentiality, and the revised PPM policy strengthens protection against reprisals," it added.

Sausmikat said Germany — as a co-founder and the fourth-largest shareholder of the AIIB — could also play a role, working with other member states to push for changes.

Hartmann also stressed that the bank's shareholders bear responsibility and urged the AIIB's Board of Directors to amend the rules governing the grievance mechanism. "We need a policy based on good-practice standards."

This article was originally written in German.

#761. DWTS' Alfonso Ribeiro Sets Record Straight on Voting Point System

After Dancing With the Stars shockingly eliminated Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson in the semi-finals, host Alfonso Ribeiro chimed in on fan speculation about how the show's ranking system works.

Alfonso Ribeiro has proof that on Dancing With the Stars, the numbers add up.

After a season of nail-biting eliminations, the DWTS host responded to a fan theory stating contestants are ranked twice in numerical order—from highest to lowest—based on their scores from the judges' panel and again from the audience vote. From there, the theory suggests each star is awarded two sets of points to match their numerical positions in each ranking.

But the Fresh Prince of Bel-Air alum shut down the assumption that two stars ranking the same—like when Amber Glenn and Jenna Dewan both earned 30 points from the judges in week nine—would result in skipping the next lowest position altogether, impacting the number of points all lower stars would receive toward escaping elimination.

"Now do the math with no breaks in the scores. It doesn’t skip 5," Ribeiro wrote Nov. 18, referring to how Harry Shum Jr. earning the highest judges' score of the seven contestants ranked him highest at number seven, followed by Glenn and Dewan tying for sixth, while placing Maura Higgins at fifth position instead of fourth. "Maura would get 5. No skip."

And since Ezra Frech, Tatyana Ali and Connor Wood all earned the same lowest score of 27 points that week, Ribeiro again clarified how they would all rank the same, in the next position behind Higgins.

As he explained, "The lowest judges scores might be 4 not 3."

In response to sharing the behind-the-scenes insights, the original poster replied, "Speechless! Ahhh making these adjustments! Thanks Alfonso!"

And it's not the only time the 55-year-old has separated fact from fiction when it comes to the competition series. He also responded to the theory that the show was rigged against certain competitors following Hayes Grier's elimination in season 21.

"No chance," Ribeiro replied to a clip of the LexLos podcast discussing speculation about manipulating the vote. "We want everyone who’s popular to stay on. It’s basic logic."

Read on to learn more about who goes in the ballroom after the cameras go down.

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones said he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality said on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last."

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show."

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

"You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody."

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together."

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay said on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'"

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna said on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner."

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

"It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well."

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again."

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers."

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee said pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and new in something different every week, so it stays interesting."

It was a spectacle many regard as the greatest meteor display on record.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Overnight Nov. 17-18, 1966, the Leonid meteor storm thrilled stargazers during one extraordinary night when the stars themselves looked as though they were falling from the sky.

At the peak of the shower, observers at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona estimated an astonishing 40 meteors per second streaking across the sky. That's 2,400 shooting stars per minute, or a staggering 144,000 per hour. It was a spectacle that many regard as the greatest meteor display in recorded history.

It's hard to imagine what it was like to experience such a spectacle. But who better to tell us than those who saw it with their own eyes? To mark the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, we asked those who saw it to share their memories.

"I was around 9 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid storm, living a few miles east of Roxie, Mississippi. We lived in a rural, dark, relatively remote area with almost zero outside lights.

"I and a couple cousins were spending the night at our Uncle and Aunt's house, staying up late, just fooling around outside like young kids do when living in the 'sticks'. As we walked down a road, I remember hearing an almost constant series of little whistling, zipping sounds. The sounds were similar to when you light a nylon rope on fire and as it burns, little flaming droplets drip down with a zippy sound.

"I looked up and the sky was filled with streaks of 'shooting stars' and I realized that was what made the sounds. I yelled at my cousins to look up and we could hardly believe what we saw. We all laid down on our backs and for a couple of hours just watched and listened to what seemed like 1000's of 'shooting stars' zipping and zinging overhead. I could even smell the sulphur-like odor from the burning little bits of space dust.

"I'm nearly 70 years old now but I'll never forget that experience. I always knew what I'd seen that night was special but not until much later in life, after the internet, did I realize just how lucky I was to have experienced that storm. That night was one of the most loved and memorable nights of my life and I'll treasure it forever."

"I was an astronomy lab assistant at Southwestern College in Winfield, KS, in 1966, majoring in physics and math and the physics professor was sure that the Leonids would be an amazing shower worth the class time.

"The sky was clear. He called me early the morning of the 17th and told me to get to the campus. I can't remember the exact time as students and faculty were pounding on doors to get people, including neighbors,to watch.

"We were all lying in an open grassy area because that was the best way to see the whole sky. It was like a humongous fireworks display and lasted even as the sun began to rise.

"As years have gone by, I have felt grateful and privileged to have seen such a wonderful astronomical event."

"I was 18 and spent the night in El Paso, Texas, lying on the ground in my backyard and watching. It looked like every star in the sky was falling. It was amazing!"

"I was 9 years old and was camping with my dad in the western mountains of California. We were set up to sleep outside, but on this particular night, we saw more meteors than I have ever seen before or since. We watched them all night and didn't get much sleep."

"Brooklyn Center, Minnesota. 14 years old. Watched in our front yard. The sky was full. It took your breath away"

"I was 3 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid meteor shower. I remember very little at that age, but watching the sky fall that night was seared in my memory.

"My family was living in Troy, Alabama, at the time. My father, a professor of psychology, was a man of science with a special love of astronomy, which he passed onto his young son.

"He drove us several miles out of town until the skies were dark, without interference from the lights of the town. Troy was much smaller then and it was easy to find dark, clear skies.

"I remember that it was a little chilly that night. My father and I stretched out on the hood of the car, the warmth of the engine radiating against our backs.

"That night was my first meteor shower, and only many years later did I learn that year's Leonids were historic. Sadly, though I bore witness to the display, we missed the true event by several hours as I grew tired by 1:00 AM, and my father had to teach class in the morning.

"I remember many bright, colorful, and long-trailed meteors. Some left 'tails' that hung in the sky for several seconds. We only experienced the beginning of the event, but it is a core memory with my father.

"That night/morning spoiled me for future meteor watches; I assumed they would all be as interesting."

Not everyone was lucky enough to witness the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966. For some, the night was memorable for an entirely different reason.

Space.com columnist Joe Rao was just 10 years old at the time, and despite eagerly anticipating the display, the weather had other ideas.

"Standing in my backyard late on a Wednesday night in the Throggs Neck section of The Bronx, cursing the heavens. My grandfather stood at my side, just shaking his head and murmuring two words over and over: 'Too bad.'

"Clouds covered the midnight sky like a fresh coat of plaster, smearing my view of the Leonids. My mom, sister and grandmother, as well as my neighbors had long since trudged to bed, leaving only Grandpa and I to gaze at a charcoal gray sky totally devoid of stars."

Rao had been looking forward to the storm ever since a visit to New York's Hayden Planetarium, where astronomer Fred C. Hess had encouraged visitors to look out for what could be a spectacular display.

But when Rao and his grandfather ventured outside, there wasn't a single star in sight.

"After a few minutes, I sobbed to my grandfather, 'But they promised it was only going to be partly cloudy tonight.' To which he sadly replied, 'I guess the party is over.'"

The Leonid meteor shower occurs every November when Earth passes through a stream of debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.

As tiny particles of comet dust enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of around 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up and produce brilliant streaks of light we know as meteors, or shooting stars.

Most years, the Leonids produce relatively modest displays with around 10 to 15 meteors per hour under ideal viewing conditions. But occasionally, Earth encounters a particularly dense trail of debris, triggering a meteor storm.

The Leonids have a long history of putting on some spectacular displays, with significant storms recorded in 1833 and 1866. And 1966 wasn't the last time the Leonids put on an extraordinary show. In 1999, 2001 and 2002, the Leonids once again reached meteor-storm levels, producing thousands of meteors per hour at their peaks. The shows aren't over yet! With comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle due to return in 2031, astronomers are already looking ahead to what the following years could bring.

A study released in August 2026 predicts potentially impressive Leonid displays in 2033 and 2034, with peak rates exceeding 1,000 meteors per hour. However, these forecasts remain uncertain, and a repeat of the extraordinary 1966 storm is far from guaranteed.

For now, we'll just have to wait and see.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#759. Bruno Mars Announces Death of Dad in Heartbreaking Post

Bruno Mars shared that his dad Peter Hernandez died at the age of 74, writing in an emotional tribute, "In my eyes he was the greatest dad in the world."

Bruno Mars knows his dad was amazing, just the way he was.

The “That’s What I Like” shared that his father Peter Hernandez died at the age of 74 and shared a heartfelt tribute to the impact he had on his life.

“Last week I got to hug my father one last time,” Mars wrote on Instagram Nov. 19. “If you’ve ever seen me talk about him I’ve always said that he’s the man that taught me everything I know, especially when it comes to music.”

The 41-year-old—whose real name is also Peter Hernandez—added that his father helped raise six children, including Mars, his sisters Tiara, Tahiti, Presley and Jaime and his brother Eric, saying, “In my eyes he was the greatest dad in the world, and I will miss him everyday until we meet again.”

Mars—whose mother Bernadette San Pedro Bayot died from a brain aneurysm in 2013 at the age of 55—concluded his message by writing, “I Love you Pops. Kiss mom up there for me.”

Alongside the emotional message, the “Just the Way You Are” singer shared a photo of himself and his father sharing an embrace in a hospital bed along with several pictures of his father from throughout the years. He did not confirm his father’s cause of death.

Mars and his dad had shared a truly special bond through the years as the “Uptown Funk” singer’s love of music was inspired by his father’s own history of performing. While Hernandez was born in Brooklyn, he later moved to Hawaii, where he founded a doo-wop revival group called The Love Notes.

And from a young age, Hernandez—who split from Mars’ mother when the Grammy winner was 12—knew that his son was destined for greatness.

“He was a ham,” Hernandez told MidWeek about Mars in 2014. “As soon as he could walk and express himself, he had to be in the middle of everything and wanted to be a part of whoever he’d seen on TV.”

Of course, he was incredibly proud that his son was “the product of a lot of love from all his family.”

“No woman could ever love Bruno as much as his late mother did,” he added, “and no man could ever love Bruno as much as I love him.”

And Hernandez was there for his son right until the end, offering Mars advice on what to say when he was honored with a Las Vegas street named after him in April.

“He says, ‘My loving son, I know you don't like advice, but getting a street named after you is a monumental moment,’” Mars recounted in a video from the event shared by AP News. “‘I just wanna say, I know you must be very proud, ‘cause I’m so proud for you. If you are gonna say anything on the mic to the crowd, both God and people love humility. So be humble and tell your fans it's their street, and you're so honored and grateful.’”

#757. You Actor Alexander Haskin Dies at Santa Monica Pier

Alexander Haskin, a personal trainer who became a background actor after leaving the Air Force, died Nov. 15 at the age of 38 after entering the ocean near the Santa Monica Pier, according to police.

Police are investigating the tragic death of Alexander Haskin.

The 38-year-old—who appeared as a background actor on shows like You and The Rookie—was pronounced dead Nov. 15 shortly after he was pulled from the ocean outside the Santa Monica Pier in Los Angeles, the Santa Monica Police Department confirmed to The Los Angeles Times.

Police said they received a report at 4:06 p.m. Nov. 15 that a man was in the water. Harbor guards responded and removed Haskin from the ocean, hoisting him onto the pier deck, where the Santa Monica Fire Department paramedics continued lifesaving measures, police spokesperson Lt. Lewis Gilmour told the Times.

Despite their efforts, Haskin was pronounced dead shortly before 5 p.m.

The actor’s cause of death was deferred, pending further investigation, according to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner’s Office records obtained by the Times.

Meanwhile, Gilmour confirmed an investigation into Haskin’s death is underway, though he said a preliminary investigation found no suspicious circumstances.

Plus, police confirmed that Haskin had been alone in the moments before entering the water, despite reports that he had been in an altercation with another person.

“The evidence shows the man was alone and did not interact with anyone in the period immediately before the incident,” Gilmour told the Times. “Security footage corroborates that finding.”

Following Haskin’s death, his dad Dana Haskin told the Times that his son had seemed in good spirits when they last spoke on Nov. 13. He also shared that Haskin had sent him a short text the morning of his death, though he did not disclose the message’s contents.

He also remembered his son—an Air Force veteran and personal trainer—as a “multifaceted guy” who loved music, fitness and acting.

“He was a happy guy,” Dana Haskin told the Times. “He liked to joke around, and he was always getting in trouble, but in a good way.”
